How to drive it

Click a point in the cloud to see that pixel's EVI series and where it sits on the ground. Drag to lasso a region and get its mean ±1 std. Promote either to an endmember, then unmix. Amber marks a region, crimson marks a single pixel, throughout.

Reading the abundance composite

Three of the fraction planes are driven into red, green and blue, so each pixel's colour is its recipe. A pure endmember shows as a saturated primary; an even mix of two shows as the secondary between them (red + green reads yellow); a pixel with none of the three stays dark. On 0–1 direct the mapping is quantitative — full brightness means 100% abundance — so patches of equal colour genuinely hold equal proportions. The 2–98% stretch pulls out faint structure but breaks that, since each channel then gets its own scale.

This is worth more than the four greyscales beside it: mixing is what the method is about, and a boundary that grades yellow → green tells you one cover type is giving way to another, which is exactly the transition four separate panels make you reconstruct in your head. With more than three endmembers you choose which three to show; the rest stay available in the strip below.

Why MNF and smoothing are on by default

These 16-day composites are noise-dominated: date-to-date jitter is nearly as large as the whole seasonal signal, and lag-1 autocorrelation is only 0.34 where smooth phenology would exceed 0.8. PCA orders components by total variance, so it happily ranks noise above signal — MNF whitens the noise first and orders by signal-to-noise instead. Turn both off and watch the cloud dissolve into a featureless blob; that is the honest picture of the raw data.

Your own imagery

Open GeoTIFF…, or drop a file anywhere on this page. It never leaves your machine — the file is read in the browser, nothing is uploaded. The reader handles what GDAL, rasterio and Earth Engine normally write: stripped or tiled, Deflate / LZW / PackBits / uncompressed, predictors 1–3, and 8/16/32-bit integer or 32/64-bit float samples. JPEG-compressed and BigTIFF files are refused by name rather than guessed at. Band descriptions of the form 2021_01_17_EVI become the date axis; otherwise bands are numbered. The stored scaling is detected, so native EVI, 0–255 stretches and ×10000 MODIS products all plot correctly.

Scenes over 150k pixels are decimated on a regular grid so the cloud stays interactive. That costs spatial detail in the map, but endmember profiles are per-pixel time series and are unaffected — the set you export is exact.

What still needs the Python tool

Writing the abundance images back out as a georeferenced float64 GeoTIFF, and running at full resolution over a whole scene: python evi_tma.py explore yours.tif. The endmember file exported here feeds it directly — evi_tma.py unmix yours.tif -e endmembers.json — so you can choose endmembers in the browser and produce the raster there. The _gee.js export runs as-is in the Earth Engine code editor. The built-in Rwanda sample is quantised to 8 bits (±0.5 DN, against ~17 DN of sensor noise); files you open are read at full precision.
